extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners in AI, blockchain, IoT, and decentralized systems (academics, industry engineers, graduate students)
extracted.subtask_description: Survey-style identification of open research challenges and design criteria for combining blockchain and AI across domains (IoT, healthcare, supply chain, robotics, finance, etc.). Focuses on technical, security, privacy, governance, and standardization requirements for decentralized AI systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Public blockchain ledgers enable secure and authentic data processing, however, collected data are publically accessible and available for all readers. Pervasive sensing systems in IoT continuously collect consumers’ personal and sensitive data and putting this data on open ledgers could lead towards privacy issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use private blockchain ledgers, encryption, and controlled access to ensure data privacy; but note the trade-off: private ledgers limit access/exposure of large datasets that AI may need for accurate decision making. Design must balance privacy protection with AI data requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scalability and Side Chains
rubrics_metrics.description: Scalability is one of the major concerns for today’s blockchain platform. Bitcoin can perform ≈4 TPS, Ethereum ≈12 TPS — far below systems like Facebook. Side chains (aka side channels) accelerate performance by settling transactions off the main chain and committing less frequently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ side chains/side channels and explore emerging blockchains with improved consensus (e.g., Algorand, IOTA). More research is needed to raise throughput and latency to levels comparable to large-scale web platforms while preserving security and decentralization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blockchain Security
rubrics_metrics.description: The decentralized power found in blockchain can suffer from abuses and misuses; blockchain systems are vulnerable to attacks such as the 51% attack. Consensus mechanisms depending on miner hashing power can be compromised, leading to centralization around a few mining farms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that private blockchains reduce some attack surfaces but introduce other risks (e.g., unprotected execution environments). Mitigations include designing robust consensus, distribution of mining power, and using Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) such as Intel SGX for protected execution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smart Contracts Vulnerabilities and Deterministic Execution
rubrics_metrics.description: It is crucial to ensure smart contract implementations are free of bugs and vulnerabilities and secure against attacks (example: DAO hack lost 3.6M ETH). Currently smart contract execution outcomes are deterministic, whereas AI/machine-learning outputs are often probabilistic, approximate, and non-deterministic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize blockchain engineering practices: rigorous testing and vulnerability assessment tools for smart contracts. Develop novel solutions for handling approximate/non-deterministic computation on-chain (e.g., consensus protocols that agree on results with specified degrees of certainty, accuracy, or precision).

rubrics_metrics.name: Trusted Oracles
rubrics_metrics.description: Smart contracts cannot pull external data on their own; oracles (trusted external parties/nodes) are used to push events and data to contracts. Oracles add complexity and a potential centralization point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design trust management for oracles (e.g., oracle voting schemes), evaluate centralization risks introduced by oracle sets, and research secure methods for integrating external data without undermining decentralization.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI-specific Emerging Consensus Protocols
rubrics_metrics.description: Existing consensus protocols consider network and middleware layers via proof-of-X protocols. There are research opportunities to design application-level consensus that consider proofs based on quality of learning models, efficient search strategies, data quality and provenance, and quality of optimization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explore consensus mechanisms that reward/model/validate AI-specific properties (model quality, provenance, dataset utility) rather than just compute or stake, enabling meaningful application-level agreement among participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fog Computing Paradigm
rubrics_metrics.description: Fog computing enables localized computing and storage close to IoT data sources (fog nodes act like local small-scale clouds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equip future fog nodes with AI and blockchain interfaces so localized management, access, and control of data can be performed near the data source to reduce cloud latency and support decentralized AI workflows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of Standards, Interoperability, and Regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Blockchain technology standards are yet to be devised. Work is in progress by IEEE, NIST, ITU and others, but governance, interoperability, integration, and architecture standards remain immature. Local and global laws, policies, and guidelines for blockchain deployment, arbitration, and dispute handling are lacking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drive research and proofs-of-concept to inform standard bodies and regulators; define technical standards for blockchain architectures, services, deployment, and interoperability, and address legal/regulatory frameworks for AI-enabled blockchain transactions (finance, automated payments, arbitration).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantum Computing
rubrics_metrics.description: Future quantum computing may break public key encryption schemes used by blockchain for digital signatures; some experts predict this could be feasible by ~2027.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research and develop quantum-safe blockchain primitives, migration strategies to quantum-resilient platforms, and interoperability models so systems remain secure and performant in a post-quantum world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governance
rubrics_metrics.description: Deploying, constructing, and managing a blockchain among diverse participants raises governance issues: which blockchain to deploy (Hyperledger vs Ethereum), who administers nodes, node deployment locations, who writes smart contracts, dispute settlement, oracle selection, off-chain mechanisms, side channel deployment, and compliance with standards/regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Devise sound governance models that cover administration, troubleshooting, smart contract authorship, dispute resolution, oracle selection, off-chain coordination, and regulatory compliance for consortium and public deployments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blockchain-based incentivization and auditability for AI services
rubrics_metrics.description: AI service providers can publish diagnostic report images and AI diagnosis outputs on the blockchain; providers can be incentivized only when diagnosis results match those of clinical radiologists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use immutable on-chain records of inputs and outputs so clinicians can compare results; design incentive mechanisms that reward accurate diagnoses to improve model quality and create auditable traces of AI service performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of existence and discovery via IPFS and smart contracts
rubrics_metrics.description: For autonomous agents/robotic swarms, discovery documents (location, time, recordings) can be stored in a decentralized file system (e.g., IPFS) and a document hash included on a blockchain smart contract. The hash provides a secure, immutable, and time-stamped record of discovery events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Store full content off-chain (IPFS) and record hashes on-chain; verify proofs by re-computing and comparing hashes. Applicable to landmine detection, disaster relief, ocean exploration, and other domains requiring tamper-evident attestations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federated/decentralized learning and data ownership for privacy (Snips AIR example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Federated learning, combined with blockchain, can improve users' privacy by ensuring data are not stored in the cloud. Snips AIR exemplifies a voice assistant that keeps personal data on-device and uses blockchain tokens to incentivize encrypted data storage and decentralized training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt decentralized learning paradigms where model training/aggregation occurs without central data pooling; use tokenization/incentives for data contribution, encrypt data, and design architectures where AI training and model provenance are managed on-chain or via decentralized coordination to protect user privacy.
